title: Museums charging for entry

turns.speaker: Kate
turns.text: The national museum is consulting on a twelve-pound entry charge. Free for under eighteens and for residents of the city.

turns.speaker: Arun
turns.text: The residents carve-out tells you they know the objection and are trying to buy it off.

turns.speaker: Delphine
turns.text: It's not a bad carve-out, mind you. Most of the visitors are tourists who paid four hundred pounds for a flight.

turns.speaker: Kate
turns.text: The evidence from the last time charges were dropped is pretty stark though. Visits roughly doubled.

turns.speaker: Arun
turns.text: Doubled in numbers. Did the mix change?

turns.speaker: Kate
turns.text: Barely. That's the finding that ought to be embarrassing. Free entry mostly gave more visits to the people already coming.

turns.speaker: Delphine
turns.text: Because the barrier was never the ticket. It's whether you were taken as a child, and whether the building looks like it's for you.

turns.speaker: Delphine
turns.text: A free door into a place you feel unwelcome in is still a closed door.

turns.speaker: Arun
turns.text: So the money would be better spent on outreach than on the door.

turns.speaker: Kate
turns.text: Possibly. Although charging does something free entry doesn't, which is make people plan and stay longer.

turns.speaker: Arun
turns.text: That's a genuine argument and it always sounds like a rationalisation.

turns.speaker: Delphine
turns.text: The practical risk is that once a charge exists it never comes off, and the free days drift to Tuesday mornings.

turns.speaker: Kate
turns.text: Which is how every concession scheme I've ever seen has ended.

points: A national museum proposes twelve-pound entry, free for under-eighteens and city residents.
Delphine notes most visitors are tourists who already paid heavily to travel.
When charges were previously dropped, visits roughly doubled but the demographic mix barely changed.
Delphine argues the real barriers are childhood exposure and whether the institution feels welcoming, not the ticket price.
Arun suggests outreach would be a better use of funds than free entry.
Kate concedes charging encourages longer, planned visits, while Delphine warns charges are rarely reversed and free access drifts to inconvenient times.
